boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten documented Princeton customs spanning first-year welcome, campus lore, athletics, Reunions, songs, and graduation week.

cards.title: Cane Spree
cards.subtitle: Princeton athletics tradition
cards.notes: Look for archival images of this class competition, and use the official Princetoniana record to place it within Princeton athletics history.
cards.short_summary: A Princeton athletic competition named among the University’s enduring traditions.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana identifies Cane Spree as one of Princeton’s athletic competitions and traditions.
cards.access_notes: Historical and event availability vary; consult Princeton Athletics for any current scheduling.

cards.title: The Big Three Bonfire
cards.subtitle: Cannon Green
cards.notes: View the official archival photographs and read why this celebration appears only after a qualifying Big Three football season.
cards.short_summary: A sporadic football-victory bonfire tied to Harvard, Yale, and Princeton results.
cards.evidence_claim: The Bonfire celebrates Princeton football having the best single-season record among the Big Three; Princetoniana says the most recent was in 2021.
cards.access_notes: Sporadic tradition; do not assume an event will occur in a given year.

cards.title: The Locomotive
cards.subtitle: Princeton cheer tradition
cards.notes: Listen for the call-and-response at an appropriate Princeton event, or compare its current form with the earlier cheers documented by Princetoniana.
cards.short_summary: Princeton’s named cheer carries a distinctive tiger-and-boom cadence.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana states that the Princeton Cheer is today called the “Locomotive” and documents its wording and history.
cards.access_notes: Participate only when invited or when it is part of a public University event.

cards.title: The P-rade
cards.subtitle: Princeton Reunions
cards.notes: Find the procession during Reunions and photograph the class-year visuals from a public viewing spot without blocking marchers.
cards.short_summary: The alumni procession that is a defining visual of Princeton Reunions.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana identifies the P-rade as the colorful spectacle of Princeton Reunions and traditions.
cards.access_notes: Occurs as part of Reunions; follow current University event guidance and public viewing rules.

cards.title: Class Jackets, Costumes, and Orange-and-Black
cards.subtitle: Princeton Reunions
cards.notes: Use official Reunions imagery to notice how returning classes make their year and shared identity visible in the parade.
cards.short_summary: Class-specific apparel and costumes give the P-rade its instantly recognizable visual language.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana maintains a dedicated record of Reunions jackets and costumes as part of the University’s traditions.
cards.access_notes: Observe or photograph only in public event areas; apparel requirements vary by class and event.

cards.title: Pre-rade: Entering Through the Gate
cards.subtitle: First-year welcome tradition
cards.notes: Follow the official route in the documentation: first-years process after Opening Exercises and enter through FitzRandolph Gate.
cards.short_summary: A first-year procession modeled after the alumni P-rade.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana dates the first Pre-rade to September 5, 2004 and says it is for first-year students only.
cards.access_notes: Part of first-year orientation; participation is limited to the University’s orientation program.

cards.title: First-Year Step Sing at Blair Arch
cards.subtitle: Blair Arch, Pre-rade finale
cards.notes: At the end of Pre-rade, first-years gather at Blair Arch to learn the alma mater; treat it as an orientation activity.
cards.short_summary: The incoming class learns “Old Nassau” together at the end of Pre-rade.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana says Pre-rade ends at Blair Arch, where freshmen take part in a Step Sing and learn “Old Nassau.”
cards.access_notes: Orientation tradition for incoming students; do not disrupt scheduled programming.

cards.title: Learning “Old Nassau”
cards.subtitle: Princeton alma mater tradition
cards.notes: Read the official song history, then recognize how its teaching is built into the first-year welcome and other Princeton ceremonies.
cards.short_summary: Princeton’s alma mater is passed to incoming students through a documented welcome practice.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana documents “Old Nassau” as Princeton’s alma mater and describes alumni teaching it to first-year students.
cards.access_notes: Use official event settings and respect performers or program leaders.

cards.title: Senior Class Step Sing
cards.subtitle: Commencement Week
cards.notes: During Commencement Week, find the Sunday-evening gathering where seniors select songs that reflect their Princeton experience.
cards.short_summary: A century-old informal senior gathering built around songs and class jackets.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana says the Senior Class Step Sing has been part of the traditional senior celebration for more than a century.
cards.access_notes: Held during Commencement Week; follow current University schedules and attendance guidance.

cards.title: The Gate You Wait to Exit
cards.subtitle: FitzRandolph Gate, Princeton campus
cards.notes: Photograph the named campus entrance and treat the graduation superstition as lore, not as a rule governing ordinary gate use.
cards.short_summary: Students have long avoided exiting through the gate before graduation because of campus lore.
cards.evidence_claim: Princetoniana says that since 1970 FitzRandolph Gate has stayed open for regular use, while many students avoid it before graduation because of lore and legend.
cards.access_notes: The gate is open for regular use; the graduation belief is documented campus lore.
